english: Wine, therefore, the unrestrained anger is; making men unrestrained; and wrath is insolent: for it arises from boiling anger. But if, according to the law, the Nazirites abstain from wine, then it has been ordained by law that the Nazirites are to be outside anger. Here Christ is plainly called a king: for the one who provokes him through sins, sins against his own soul. Just as the foolish man is not ashamed of disgrace, so the one who borrows grain to sow in an unplowed field: already, because it will be repaid from his farm to the lender, even if the borrower should happen to die. — If it is possible to borrow grain in an unplowed field from those who have worked their own land in the six years, that is, from those righteous ones and prophets who shone in the six ages before Christ’s presence, to imitate their virtues, those who also nourish in the seventh year the widow and the orphan, in order to repay them in the kingdom of heaven the reward of the manifestation of virtues, having become firstfruits of the virtues. Those whom, clearly by virtue, someone has begotten, will leave to those who come after an icon 17.212 and a blessing; and the unblemished one will leave righteousness of nurture until the end. For elsewhere it was said that the one who speaks evil ceases; but also Christ: and the one who reviles the Church will be deprived of the faith, which was to him light before the slander; and he would also speak concerning the outer darkness; therefore it has been said concerning the future: and Christ himself, father and mother, is able to be spoken of: father indeed of those who have the Spirit of adoption; mother however of those who need milk and not solid food.

And indeed, the Christ who speaks in Paul—though He is the one speaking—was made a father to the Ephesians, revealing to them the mysteries of wisdom; and He became a mother to the Corinthians, nourishing them with milk. The pleasure discovered among us that comes from evil, which he says is assigned as a portion in the first things, at first delights your palate, but later you will find it more bitter than gall. Do not speak, moved by pride: “I alone will wage war against my enemies”; but wait for the Lord and call upon Him, that He may help you. Do not rely on yourself as if you could act without the Lord; for He says through David that apart from Him there is no helper: “I do not trust in my bow.” Regarding sensible things, we say that a large and small weight exists—among which are gold, silver, bronze, lead, and whatever else is weighed. Measures, however, are those things measured in vessels: grain, wine, oil, and legumes. Furthermore, the person called bold yet timid by some, I consider to be a large and small weight. Moreover, universally, every excess and deficiency—this is a large and small weight; for both are vices, and measures are doubled. Furthermore, the one who wishes to suffer well at the hands of others, yet himself does not choose to similarly relieve others, possesses double measures—namely, not obeying the command that says: “Whatever you wish that people would do to you, you also do to them.” Not the ear that hears badly is the work of the Lord, but the one who attends to good things; and not the eye that sees badly is the work of the Lord, but the one who sees and imagines divine things.

For whoever hears the Lord and observes his commandments performs the work of the Lord. The same principle applies to all parts of the body. You should employ this statement against those who accuse us, saying that our body and the God within us are engaging in insolence. This means: do not sleep excessively, but remain wakeful, so that you may not be cast into Gehenna. Do not slander. Through the virtues, open the eyes of your soul. Through wisdom, be filled with heavenly bread. To weigh oneself against the works of the Lord and also 17.213 of the devil’s works is an abomination to the Lord. Yet the Lord calls a balance-scale the mind, which is naturally endowed to judge rightly the things that occur, but which is inclined by the impulse of self-will through friends or riches. Do not hasten, he says, toward the promise before God, lest the need, or the desire of the greater abundance, seize you and begin to repent, and you insult God by preferring something else to him. For repentance upon good things does not happen to the just, but to the unjust. The unjust, therefore, should not make any promise to God without careful consideration, for after praying, repentance arises. –To hastily dedicate oneself to the Lord, which is to sanctify something of one’s own, and then immediately afterward to change one’s mind, is a snare to the man. Christ is the winnower of the godless. He will come upon the godless like a lion upon prey. Or a winnowing fan, which separates the chaff from the grain, he will apply to them.

english: An absurd punishment. The mind is the storehouse of the belly, the heart, and knowledge; in it are laid up all divine teachings as well as impious doctrines. Just as one who lights a lamp seeks to find something among the things stored in the pantries, so the Lord, with the light of His knowledge, searches the storehouses of human words and deeds. To those people who know the Lord’s knowledge, it is light for them. Therefore, if the Lord’s light is the Lord’s knowledge, and the Lord’s light is the breath of humanity, then the Lord’s knowledge is the breath of humanity. The demon who appears in ignorance, pretending to be something, He has named a lamp that empties the mind of good knowledges and transforms itself into an angel of light. Since, however, the Lord’s light was not chosen to be known or walked in by them, the impious reckoned ignorance as light. If they indeed held ignorance as light, then clearly they also practiced the works invented by the demon of ignorance; those who journeyed with his ignorance will be with him into the ages of ages. But those who are with the Lord’s knowledge will be with the Lord. He casts out this statement regarding the sacrifice offered through irrational beasts; for a sacrifice to God is a spirit broken in pieces. If holy and right works are the Lord’s works, and one of His works is the mind,

The mind was rightly created by God, pure and upright, and we are obligated to preserve it in that state against the evil influences that come upon us. He set the defiled and common house in opposition to the open-air corner; but if the defiled and common house is wickedness, then the open-air corner is virtue—the very angle of virtue. This is the practice of contemplation in action, touching and enlightened by the sun of righteousness. Paul also spoke well when he called the high priest of the Jews a defiled wall, to be struck blind by God. Likewise, the Savior in the Gospels called the Pharisees defiled tombs. And well did he say in verse 17.216, upon the corner: “Here lies the stone rejected by the builders, which has become the cornerstone; and this is Christ.” Now, what is common is what does not belong to the one God. Secret giving is when the right hand acts and the left hand does not know; it stirs up a strong wrath against itself on the day of judgment, the one who withholds aid from the needy. The synagogue of the giants is wickedness and ignorance; for the giants are the demons. This means that the one who strays from the path of righteousness will find rest in great sins. It is better to be solitary than to keep company with such as these; and David says: “In a desolate, impassable, and waterless land, thus have I appeared before you in the holy place.”

The earth is now a desert where virtue dwells in the soul, uninhabited by the old human passions that once dwelled there—those corrupting impulses that once ruled according to the former deceitful desires. For this reason, the devil finds no rest in it, since he wanders wearily through waterless places seeking repose, yet finds none; for he is king over all who dwell in the waters, that is, over those who rest and indulge in carnal pleasures. Again: the paths of wisdom are the sheltered dwellings of her house. If this is so, then surely the warlike, gossiping, wrathful woman is wickedness itself—the kind that makes the one who lives with her become warlike, gossipy, and irritable. Wisdom of the Lord rests in the heart of a righteous, wise person; but foolish men slander her in order to destroy her. Wisdom is a fortified city, within which the wise dwell, tearing down reasonings and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God—of which the fortified cities, says the text, are those souls subdued and conquered by impious demons and wicked men, who exalt themselves against the knowledge of God. When the wise man ascends this stronghold and sees their supposed security, he, by means of such wisdom, surrounds and overthrows it. He who guards mouth, tongue, mind, passion, and desire preserves his soul from the anguish of judgment. He himself is…

english: One who devises schemes in his mind: bold, indeed, is the one who undertakes anything without fear; self-willed, the one who desires to act freely without examination; boastful, the one who exalts himself beyond what he truly possesses in dignity; a plague, the one who, while destroying himself, also transmits harm to others—for such a one is destructive in nature, so as to spread wickedness to others as well; and whoever cherishes grudges is lawless. For there is also a good desire: the angels, therefore, are those who never at any time desire evil desire; the demons, those who continually desire evil things; human beings, those who at times desire, and at times do not desire; and the one who desires the whole day through, instead of throughout the whole of life—such is also the meaning of, “In the fear of the Lord, be vigilant all the day,” in place of “throughout the whole of life.” 17.217 He says the horse is the mind, the one engaged in battle against the devil, and opposing him; for, he says, “You shall mount upon your horses,” and “your horsemanship shall be salvation,” and concerning the Lord upon Paul: “That you may stand firm in my name,” he says. He named the virtue signified by a familiar name a good name; for this too is good—the name, which possesses a good meaning. Thus, we do not praise the unjust woman called Justice, but the one who possesses justice, even if injustice is thought to be hers; and above silver and gold, heavenly wisdom. They meet one another: the rich, by means of acts of mercy, purges his anger and acquires love; but the other, through poverty, is taught humility of mind. For the one wishes to be instructed; the other, to give instruction—so that the one may be joyful, the other merciful. He who possesses wisdom and the fear of the Lord shall inherit heavenly life, glory, and wealth.

For Noah possessed every generation; Abraham possessed these as well; and those who were taught by Peter also possessed them. In the age to come, those who have been enriched in every way, in all knowledge and wisdom, will rule over the ungrateful and the deprived of this wealth—but as for who are the servants and who are the masters, it is not necessary to make this public, because the discourse concerning them is mystical and profound; and even to make it explicit, they demonstrate the instability of human life. Yet even in oligarchies, the rich rule over the poor; and otherwise, those who possess knowledge rule over those who are not such; and the faithful from among the Gentiles, to the Israelites to whom they had previously lent, now lend teaching—but formerly they had lent to many nations and ruled over them; now, however, since the kingdom has been taken from them, the reverse has come to pass. God loves the cheerful man in the commandments, and the giver in acts of mercy, as Paul also says: “He who shows mercy, in cheerfulness”; and the Lord brings to completion the vanity of works through virtue and through knowledge. Human gifts—namely, the virtues of the soul—He names, by means of which, conquering the devil, one provides oneself as precious to God, and deprives oneself of the soul from those demons who have acquired it. He desires that the person be cast out from the habit of the hand by means of spiritual teaching, with which he once had contentiousness; and the demon, being a plague of the soul, must be chased forth—for if he dwells within it, through impurity he dishonors all the right reasonings.

For indeed, the apostle shows that the soul is like a council, bringing in thoughts either as accusers or as those making a defense; for he says, "Between one another, the thoughts are either accusing or defending." And where there is accusation and defense, there is also a council. But also, the plague dishonors all as a tyrant, or as one who wishes to establish his own customs, casting out the customs of others in disgrace, whom he has cast out from a spiritual system; and not only will he himself be cast out, but also those associated with him—quarrels, contentions, battles, and all that produces plague. The Lord who guards our souls also shepherds our spiritual knowledge, coming down and saying, "I am the good shepherd, whom the lawless one dishonors." But if Christ is indeed king of those who are ruled, and shepherd of the flock, then he will one day be alone king of the flock, when those worthy of the royal dignity pass into the royal state. Our enemy, the devil, walks about like a lion seeking whom he may devour; whom the timid, fearing, takes up into the labor of virtues. But if the lion is on the paths of justice seeking to seize someone, that one is the devil; and in the broad ways leading to destruction, with his phalanx of demons, he himself slays those who obey him. The devil is a deep pit; but the one hated by the Lord, who does not attend to himself securely—yet Job was not hated by the Lord, but was undergoing trial.

καρδίας τοῦ ἄφρονός ἐστιν ἡ ῥάβδος ἡ ἐκ τῆς ῥίζης Ἰεσσαὶ ὁ Χριστὸς, ὃς ποιμανεῖ τὸν
λαὸν αὐτοῦ τὸν νέον Ἰσραὴλ ἐν τῇ νομῇ τῶν ἑαυ τοῦ προβάτων. Ὥσπερ ὁ διάβολος
συκοφαντεῖ ἡμᾶς πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν, λαμβάνων παρ' ἡμῶν τὰς ἀρετὰς, ἃς μὴ δέδωκεν
ἡμῖν, οὕτω καὶ ἡμεῖς συκοφαντοῦμεν αὐτὸν λαμβά νοντες παρ' αὐτοῦ τὰς κακίας ἃς
μὴ δεδώκαμεν αὐτῷ· καὶ καθὸ μὲν λαμβάνομεν παρ' αὐτοῦ τὰς κακίας, ὡς παρὰ
πένητος ἐν ἀρεταῖς λαμβάνομεν· καθὸ δὲ τὰς ἀρετὰς ἡμῶν διδόαμεν αὐτῷ ἐπ'
ἐλαττώσει ἡμῶν, ὡς πλουσίῳ ἐν κακίᾳ διδόαμεν· μήποτε δὲ, φησὶν, ὡς ὀλίγα διδοὺς
ἄρχοντι· παρ' ᾧ συκοφαντεῖ τὰ πλείω κερδαίνων, πλέον καὶ βλάπτεται τὴν ψυχήν.
Ὁ τοῖς πανσόφοις λόγοις προσέχων τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ ποιῶν τὰ προστασσόμενα ὑπ'
αὐτοῦ, οὗτος ἐπέστησε τὴν καρδίαν, καὶ ἔγνω ὅτι καλοί εἰσιν· οὗτος ἀκούει τῶν τοῦ
Θεοῦ λόγων, ὁ ποιῶν τὰ προστασσόμενα ὑπ' αὐτῶν· Οὐ γὰρ οἱ ἀκροαταὶ τοῦ νόμου
δίκαιοι παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ, ἀλλ' οἱ ποιηταὶ τοῦ νόμου δικαιωθήσον ται. Ἐὰν δὲ ἐπιστήσῃς
σὴν καρδίαν τοῦ γνῶναι καὶ ποιῆσαι, γνωρίσει σοι τὴν ὁδὸν αὐτοῦ τὴν εἰποῦσαν·
Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ὁδὸς καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια. Ὁ πλατύνας διὰ τῆς καθαρότητος τὴν καρδίαν αὑ
τοῦ, νοήσει τοὺς τοῦ Θεοῦ λόγους, τούς τε πρακτι κοὺς, καὶ τοὺς σοφιστικοὺς, καὶ
τοὺς θεολογικούς· πᾶσα γὰρ ἡ κατὰ τὴν Γραφὴν πραγματεία, τέμνεται τριχῶς, εἰς
ἠθικὴν καὶ φυσικὴν καὶ θεολογικήν· καὶ ἀκολουθεῖ τῇ μὲν πρώτῃ, αἱ Προοιμίαι· τῇ
δὲ δευ τέρᾳ, ὁ Ἐκκλησιαστής· τῇ δὲ τρίτῃ, Ἄσμα ᾀσμάτων· 17.221 ἅπερ νοηθέντα διὰ
καθαρότητος ἐναπογράφεται τῇ καρδίᾳ, τοῦ ἀποκρίνασθαί σε, ὡς ἕτοιμον εἶναι πρὸς
ἀπολογίαν παντὶ τῷ ἐπερωτῶντί σε λόγον περὶ τῆς ἐν σοὶ ἐλπίδος· εἴτε διὰ τὸ
μαθεῖν, εἴτε διὰ τὸ ἀντιτιθεῖναι· ἀντερώτα δὲ καὶ σὺ τοὺς δυναμένους ἐρωτᾶσθαι· μὴ
μέντοι βιάζου τὸν ἐν γνώσει πε νόμενον· διὸ ἐπάγει· Καὶ μὴ ἀτιμάσῃς ἀσθενῆ ἐν
πύλαις. Οἱ τοὺς φαύλους ἀναδεχόμενοι λογισμοὺς, καὶ ἐν τού τῳ τιμῶντες τὸν
πονηρὸν, σπουδαζέτωσαν ὅση δύναμις διὰ τῶν ἀγαθῶν λογισμῶν ἀποδιδόναι τοὺς
χείρονας· ἐὰν γὰρ μὴ ἰσχύσωσι τοῦτο ποιῆσαι, λήψονται τὸ στρῶ μα τὸ ὑπὸ τὰς
πλευρὰς τῆς ψυχῆς, τουτέστι τὴν ἀρετήν. Ὁ μετατιθεὶς τὰ ὅρια τῆς θεοσεβείας,
δεισιδαιμο νίαν ἢ ἀσέβειαν αὐτὴν ἀποδείκνυσι· καὶ ὁ μετατιθεὶς τὰ ὅρια τῆς
ἀνδρείας, θρασύτητα ἢ δειλίαν αὐτὴν ἀπεργάζεται· ὡσαύτως δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἄλλων
ἀρετῶν, καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν δογμάτων, καὶ ἐπ' αὐτῆς τῆς πίστεως νοητέον· μάλιστα δὲ τοῦτο
τηρητέον ἐπὶ τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος· ὁ γὰρ μὴ θεολογῶν τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, δια λύει τὸ
βάπτισμα· ὁ δὲ καὶ ἄλλους τινὰς ὀνομάζων θεοὺς, δῆμον εἰσάγει θεῶν· ἢ καὶ τὰς περὶ
πράγμα τος ἑκάστου πατρικὰς διατάξεις, καὶ τούτου χάριν μένειν ὀφειλούσας, μὴ
μετακινεῖν δεῖ. ∆υνάστην ἐνταῦθα τὸν διάβολόν φησιν· τράπεζαι δὲ αὐτοῦ εἰσι
ψευδομαρτυρίαι, λοιδορίαι, καταλαλιαὶ, συμβουλίαι κακαὶ, ἐπιθυμίαι αἰσχραὶ, καὶ
πᾶν ὁτιοῦν σατανικὸν ἐπιτήδευμα· ταῦτα δὲ παρατιθέμενά σοι ὑπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ,
νοητῶς νόει, καὶ ἐπίβαλε τὴν διά νοιάν σου, ὅ ἐστιν ἡ χείρ· εἰδὼς ὅτι τοιαῦτά σε δεῖ
παρασκευάσαι, οἷα καὶ συμπαρεστάναι σοι ὀφείλουσιν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ Κυρίου, ὅτε
ἀπονέμει ἑκάστῳ κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ· εἰ δὲ ἀπληστότερος εἶ, καὶ ὀρέγῃ τῶν ὑψηλῶν
καὶ πλειόνων καὶ μειζόνων, ἅτινά εἰσι θεῖα καὶ Θεοῦ, μὴ ἐπιθύμει τῶν τοῦ πονηροῦ
ἐδεσμάτων· ταῦτα γὰρ ἔχεται ζωῆς προσκαίρου, ὅ ἐστι ψευδοῦς· δεῖ δὲ τὴν θείαν
Γραφὴν νοητῶς νοεῖσθαι καὶ πνευματικῶς· ἡ γὰρ κατὰ τὴν ἱστορίαν αἰσθητὴ γνῶσις,
οὐκ ἔστιν ἀληθής. Ἐὰν ἑλκῦσαι τὸν θεῖον νοῦν πρὸς τὸ ῥητὸν κατὰ τὴν ἔξω μόνον
ὅρασιν ἐθελήσῃς, ἀσύστατος ὢν εἰς τὸν ἴδιον οἶκον ἀποφοίτα, ὅς ἐστι τὸ
κατάλληλον αὐτοῦ θεώρημα· πτέρυγας ἔχων τὰς ὑπὸ τοῦ προεστηκότος αὐτοῦ ἁγίου
Πνεύματος κατασκευασθείσας αὐτῷ, αἵπερ εἰσὶ τὰ πνευματικὰ χαρίσματα· ἄπεισιν
οὖν ὑψηλὸς ὑπὲρ αὐτὸν ὡς εἰπεῖν τὸν αἰθέρα· τὸ οὖν μὴ ὑπεράνω 17.224 χωρεῖν τοῦ
ῥητοῦ, ἀλλ' ἀπλήστως ἔχειν πρὸς αὐτὰ, ζωῆς ἐστι ψευδοῦς. Εἰ ὁ βάσκανος σῖτα
ἀσεβείας ἐσθίει, καὶ οἴνῳ πα ρανόμῳ μεθύσκεται, οὐ δεῖ δὲ συνδειπνεῖν τούτῳ· οὐ
χρὴ ἄρα εἶναι ἀσεβῆ καὶ παράνομον· αὗται γὰρ αἱ κακίαι λυμαίνονται γνῶσιν
πνευματικήν. Μηδὲν λέγε συνετὸν, φησὶ, τουτέστι βαθὺ καὶ μυστι κόν· οὐ δεῖ γάρ σε
βαλεῖν τοὺς μαργαρίτας ἔμπροσθεν τῶν χοίρων. Ὅρια αἰώνια θεοσεβείας μὴ μέταιρε·
english: Grace is for the one whose mouth has fallen into iniquity; but the one hated by the Lord is left in the pit to the end, being a lover of pleasure in the knowledge of sin. The rod from the root of Jesse, which is Christ, is far from the heart of the fool; he shepherds his people, the young Israel, in the pasture of his own sheep. Just as the devil slanders us before God, taking from us virtues which he did not give us, so we slander him, taking from him evils which we did not give him. And inasmuch as we receive evils from him, we receive them as from a poor man among virtues; and inasmuch as we give our virtues to him with a lessening of ourselves, we give them as to a rich man in wickedness. But perhaps, he says, as one giving little to a ruler, from whom the slanderer gains more by accusing the greater, he gains more and damages his own soul. The one who attends to the all-wise words of God and does what he commands has established his heart and knows that they are good; this one hears the words of God, the one who does what is commanded by them. For not the hearers of the law are just before God, but the doers of the law will be justified. But if you set your heart to know and to do, he will make known to you his way, saying: I am the way and the truth. The one who enlarges his heart through purity will understand the words of God, both the practical and the sophistical.

And the theological as well: for all treatment according to Scripture is divided into three parts, into the ethical, the physical, and the theological. And to the first part belong the Prooemia; to the second, Ecclesiastes; to the third, the Song of Songs. These, when understood through purity, are inscribed in the heart, so that you may be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason for the hope that is in you, whether to learn or to refute. And you too shall ask questions of those who are able to be questioned. But do not force the one who is being led on in knowledge. Therefore he adds: And do not despise the weak in the gates. Those who accept vain reasonings, and in this way honor the wicked, let them strive with all their power, by means of good reasonings, to repay the worse. For if they are not able to do this, they will take the couch that is under the ribs of the soul, that is, virtue. The one who transfers the boundaries of piety makes it either superstition or impiety; and the one who transfers the boundaries of courage makes it either rashness or cowardice. Likewise also concerning the other virtues, and concerning the dogmas, and concerning faith itself, this must be understood. But especially must this be observed concerning the Holy Trinity. For the one who does not theologize about the Holy Spirit dissolves baptism; and the one who also names certain others as gods brings in a multitude of gods; or even the familial arrangements concerning each thing, and for this reason it is necessary to remain, not to move them. Here he declares the devil to be a potentate; but his tables are false testimonies.

Insults, slander, evil counsel, shameful desires, and every satanic practice—these the Evil One sets before you; perceive them with your intellect, and place upon them the discernment of your mind, which is your hand. Know that you must prepare yourself for such things, for they ought to stand beside you on the Day of the Lord, when He renders to each according to his works. But if you are insatiable, and reach for the lofty, the greater, and the more abundant—those things which are divine and of God—do not crave the provisions of the Evil One; for these are held fast to a fleeting life, which is falsehood. Yet you must perceive the Divine Scripture intellectually and spiritually; for the knowledge gained through historical sensation is not true. If you seek to draw the divine mind toward the literal, according to outward vision alone, you, being unstable, will depart to your own house—namely, the vision fitting to it—having wings constructed for you by the Holy Spirit who precedes you, which wings are the spiritual gifts; thus you soar high above it, as it were, into the ether. Therefore, not to comprehend the literal beyond measure, but to cling to it without satiety, is a life of falsehood. If the slanderer eats the grain of impiety and is made drunk by lawless wine, you must not dine with him; you ought not to be impious and lawless. For these vices defile spiritual knowledge. Do not speak, says he, that which is prudent—meaning deep and mysterious—for you must not cast pearls before swine. Do not transgress the eternal boundaries of godliness.

εἰς δὲ γῆν τῶν ἀπορφανισάντων ἑαυτοὺς ἀπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ, κτῆμα δὲ δαιμόνων τὴν
κακίαν ἔχοντας, μὴ εἰσέλθῃς, δι' ἣν ἐστερήθησαν τοῦ ἐπουρανίου Πατρός· ὁ γὰρ
λυτρού μενος αὐτοὺς Κύριος ἐκ τοῦ ὑπερλάμπρου φωτὸς ἀπὸ σκότους, ἰσχυρός ἐστιν.
Υἱὸς ὀρθὸς ἐνδιατρίψει τὰ χείλη αὐτοῦ σοφίᾳ, καὶ ἡ σοφία πρὸς αὐτὸν συλλαλήσει
καὶ διαμενεῖ· ὁ δὲ στρεβλὸς ἐκπεσεῖται ἀπ' αὐτῆς. Εἰ τῷ φόβῳ Κυρίου ἐκκλίνει τις
ἀπὸ κακοῦ, καλῶς παραινεῖ διὰ πάσης τῆς ζωῆς ἐκκλίνειν ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ παντὸς κακοῦ.
Πᾶς ὁ ἐν κακίᾳ μέθυσος, καὶ ὁ ἐκ σοφίας πρὸς ἀγνωσίαν καταπορνεύων, πτωχεύσει
ἐκ θείας χάριτος· καὶ οὐκ ἐνδύσεται ἔνδυμα τοῦ γάμου πᾶς ὁ ἐν τῇ δαι μονιώδει
νυκτὶ ὑπνώδης, ἀλλὰ τὴν ὡς ῥάκος τετραυ ματισμένην σάρκα διαθλίβων γεέννης
φλόγα. Ἔφη τις τῶν γερόντων, τὴν ψυχὴν εἶναι μητέρα τοῦ νοῦ, ψυχὴν λέγων τὸ
παθητικὸν τῆς ψυχῆς, θυμόν τε καὶ ἐπιθυμίαν· διὰ γὰρ τῶν πρακτικῶν ἀρετῶν εἰς
φῶς προάγει τὸν νοῦν· διὰ γὰρ ἀνδρείας καὶ σωφρο σύνης κτώμεθα σοφίαν καὶ
γνῶσιν Θεοῦ, αἵπερ εἰσὶν ἀρεταὶ θυμοῦ καὶ ἐπιθυμίας· λέγει δ' ἂν ἴσως μητέρα καὶ
τὴν παλαιὰν ∆ιαθήκην οὐ καταφρόνητον. Ἀνθρώπους ἐνταῦθα, τῶν διδασκάλων
τὰς συγγρα φάς φησι· τοὺς δὲ ποιήσαντας καὶ διδάξαντας, καὶ τὴν πορείαν πρὸς
οὐρανοὺς ποιησαμένους, περιπά τους ὠνόμασε· πολλοὶ γὰρ διδάξαντες, οὐ πρὸς
οὐρα νὸν τὴν πορείαν ἐποιήσαντο, ὅτι οὐκ ἐφύλαξαν· ὁ γὰρ ὁμιλῶν ἐν περιπάτοις,
τουτέστι ποιεῖν τε καὶ διδά σκειν, ἀξίως περιπατεῖ τῆς κλήσεως ἧς ἐκλήθη ὑπὸ τοῦ
Θεοῦ. Ἡ μὲν κατὰ διάνοιαν ἁμαρτία ἔοικε φιάλῃ· ἡ δὲ κατ' ἐνέργειαν, ποτηρίῳ·
ὕπερον δέ ἐστι, τὸ παρὰ τοῖς μαγείροις λεγόμενον τριβεύς· πολλὰ γὰρ κρούει τοῦτο
τὸ ὕπερον, καὶ οὐκ ἀνοίγει τὸν τόπον ὃν κρούει· τοῖς δὲ μαθηταῖς ὁ Κύριός φησι·
Κρούετε, καὶ ἀνοι γήσεται ὑμῖν. Νοῦς δεξάμενος ἀλλότριον νόημα ἢ μάθησιν, μελε
τήσει λογισμοὺς κακούς· ὁ δὲ τηρήσας ἑαυτὸν, κληρο νομήσει ζωήν. ∆εινὸν ἡ
ἀναλγησία· εἶτα ἐρεῖς τυπτόμενος τὴν συν είδησιν, οὐκ ἐπόνεσα φροντίσαι τῶν μὲν
γερῶν τυχεῖν, ῥυσθῆναι δὲ τῶν βασάνων· ἐνέπαιξάν μοι, 17.225 τουτέστι
προσωνείδισάν μοι· ἐγὼ δὲ θέλων οὐκ ᾔδειν πότε ὄρθρος ψυχῆς, καὶ ἐπίγνωσις
ἁμαρτίας. Ὁ οἶκος τῶν ἀρετῶν μετὰ θείας σοφίας οἰκοδομεῖ ται, καὶ μετὰ συνέσεως
φόβου Θεοῦ καὶ γνώσεως ἀνορθοῦται. Ὁ περὶ τὴν πίστιν, ἤ τινα τῶν ἀρετῶν
ναυαγῶν, ἀκυβέρνητος πρὸς πόλεμον τῶν ἀντικειμένων δυνά μεων, τῇ τε θεολογίᾳ
καὶ ταῖς ἀρεταῖς· ὁ δὲ μετὰ κυβερνήσεως πολεμῶν, ἔοικεν ἐπὶ γῆς νοῦν ἔχειν
προηγεῖται δὲ τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ βοηθείας, καρδία βουλευ τικὴ, ἡ πάντα μετὰ βουλῆς
ποιοῦσα· δυνατὸν δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ πάσης ἀρετῆς τὸ αὐτὸ τοῦτο εἰπεῖν· ἔστι γὰρ καὶ περὶ
σωφροσύνην ναυάγιον, καὶ περὶ ἀγάπην, καὶ φιλαργυρίαν, καὶ περὶ ἕκαστον δὲ
δόγμα ὁμοίως τῆς καθολικῆς καὶ ἀποστολικῆς Ἐκκλησίας συμβαίνει ναυ άγιον· εἰ δὲ
μετὰ κυβερνήσεως πολεμεῖν δεῖ τοῖς ἀντικειμένοις, ναυμαχίᾳ παραπλήσιος ἡμῖν
ἐστιν ὁ βίος ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς· ἐὰν γὰρ θέλωμεν ἡμεῖς, ποντίζομεν αὐτοὺς ἐν προσευχῇ
καρδίας, καὶ διανοίᾳ πρὸς Θεὸν τετραμμένῃ· ἐὰν δὲ μὴ θέλωμεν, ποντιζόμεθα· ἐὰν δὲ
καὶ πολεμούμεθα ὑπ' ἐκείνων, εἰ καὶ πολὺς καὶ σφοδρὸς ὁ πόλεμος αὐτῶν, οὐθέν
ἐστι· νηστείᾳ μόνον καὶ ἐγκρατείᾳ περιφράξωμεν ἑαυτοὺς, καὶ ὡς ἀράχνην αὐτούς
τε καὶ τὰ ὅπλα αὐτῶν συγκόψομεν· ἐὰν δὲ κα τὰ τὴν τοῦ Κυρίου φωνὴν, ὅπου εἰσὶ
δύο ἢ τρεῖς, ἡ καρδία, ὁ νοῦς, καὶ ἡ ψυχὴ, συμφωνήσουσι δὲ ἐν ἐν τολαῖς αὐτοῦ
περιέχεσθαι, ὁ Κύριος μεθ' ἡμῶν. Πάντα γὰρ ὅσα πράττει ὁ Θεὸς νοοῦντες, καὶ ὅσα
διδάσκει πράττοντες, κατ' οὐδὲν παραβαίνουσι τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ· πύλαι δὲ σοφῶν αἱ
πρακτικαί εἰσιν ἀρε ταὶ, καὶ ἡ τοῦ νοῦ θεωρία, δι' ὧν εἰσέρχεται σοφία Θεοῦ· οὐκ
ἐκκλίνουσι δὲ, οὔτε δεξιὰ οὔτε ἀριστερὰ, ὅτι λογίζονται ἐν συνεδρίοις εἶναι καλοῦ
καὶ κακοῦ· καὶ τοῦ μὲν καλοῦ ἀντιποιοῦνται, τὸ δὲ κακὸν προσ ακοντοῦσιν. Τοῖς μὴ
θέλουσιν ὑπὸ τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ σοφίαν καὶ γνῶσιν παιδευθῆναι, διὰ τοῦ ἐνεστῶτος
θανάτου συν αντᾷ ὁ αἰώνιος· ἄφρων δέ ἐστιν ὁ γλυκανθεὶς μὲν ἐν σοφίᾳ Θεοῦ, εἶτα
καταλιπὼν αὐτὴν, τῇ δὲ ἀφροσύνῃ συνάξει· διὸ καὶ συναπέθανεν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις· εἰ
δὲ ἀρετὴν ἡ κακία μειοῖ, καὶ τὴν κακίαν δηλονότι ἡ ἀρετὴ διαφθείρει· τοῦτο δὲ
γενήσεται ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι αἰῶνι, ἕως ἂν ἐκλίπῃ ἡ κακία· τὸ γὰρ ἐμμολυνθήσεται,
ἀντὶ τοῦ, διαφθαρήσεται· διαφθείρεται δὲ ἡ ἀκαθαρσία, ἤτοι ὑπὸ πρακτικῆς, ἢ ὑπὸ
δριμείας κολάσεως. Χρηστέον τούτῳ τῷ ῥητῷ πρὸς τοὺς καταξιωθέντας θείας
english: Do not enter the land of those who have orphaned themselves from God, who hold wickedness as a possession of demons, from whom they were deprived of the heavenly Father; for the Lord who redeems them from the surpassingly brilliant light out of darkness is mighty. A righteous son will ponder his lips with wisdom, and wisdom will speak with him and remain with him; but the twisted one will fall away from her. If one turns away from evil by the fear of the Lord, he rightly urges us through all of life to turn away from every evil. Every person drunk in wickedness, and the one who from wisdom prostitutes himself into ignorance, will become impoverished from divine grace; and he will not put on the wedding garment—every one who in the demonic night is drowsy with sleep, but instead, wearing his flesh as a ragged and torn garment, he will torment himself with the fire of Gehenna. One of the elders said: the soul is the mother of the mind, speaking of the soul as the passive part of the soul—anger and desire—for through practical virtues he advances the mind into light; for by courage and self-control we acquire wisdom and knowledge of God, which are virtues of anger and desire; he might also say that the mother is the ancient Covenant, which is not to be despised. Here, concerning the teachers, he says of their writings: but those who made them and taught them, and who made the journey toward heaven, he called wanderers; for many have taught, but they did not make their journey toward heaven, because they did not guard it; for the one who converses in walks—that is, who acts and teaches—walks worthily of the calling to which he was called by God.

Sin is like a bowl when it exists only in thought, but when it is carried out in action, it becomes like a cup that holds the deed. The overreaching part, however, is what cooks call the pestle: it strikes many blows against the substance it hits, yet it does not open the place it strikes. To His disciples, the Lord says: Knock, and it shall be opened to you. A mind that receives a foreign thought or teaching will dwell on evil reasoning; but the one who guards himself will inherit life as an inheritance. How dreadful is insensitivity to pain! Then you will say, while being struck in the conscience, that you did not strive to attain the rewards of old age, nor to be freed from torments; they mocked me, 17.225—that is, they insulted me—but I, desiring not to know when the dawn of the soul comes, nor when the recognition of sin arrives. The house of virtues, built with divine wisdom, is constructed and, with understanding, the fear of God and knowledge, is set upright. The one concerning faith, or any of the virtues that are shipwrecked, is an unskilled pilot heading into battle against opposing forces, both in theology and in virtue; but the one who sails with skill in warfare seems to possess the mind on earth that anticipates God’s help, a counseling heart, the heart that does all things with counsel; and it is possible to say the same thing regarding every virtue: for there is also shipwreck concerning temperance, and concerning love, and concerning greed, and concerning every single doctrine, which likewise happens to the catholic and apostolic Church; but if, with skill in warfare, one must fight against the opponents, then our life upon the earth is like a naval battle; for if we wish, we overwhelm them in prayer of the heart and in reason directed toward God, composed and ordered.

If we do not wish to resist, we are swept away like those who drift upon the waters; and if we are also made to war against them, even if their war is great and fierce, it amounts to nothing; we shall fortify ourselves solely by fasting and self-control, and we shall cut them off and their weapons as a spider severs its web; and if we also hearken to the voice of the Lord, wherever two or three are gathered—heart, mind, and soul— they shall agree together in being contained within His bounds, and the Lord will be with us. For all that God does, when we understand it, and all that He teaches, when we put it into practice, in no way transgress His word; the gates of wisdom are the practical deeds, and the contemplation of the mind, through which the wisdom of God enters; they do not turn aside, neither to the right nor to the left, because they reckon themselves to be in councils discerning good and evil; and they counterfeit the good, while they approach the evil. To those who do not wish to be instructed by the wisdom and knowledge of God, through the present death the eternal stands opposed; the foolish one is he who has been sweetened in the wisdom of God, then forsaken it, and now joins himself to folly; therefore he also perished with his sins; but if virtue diminishes wickedness, then wickedness is clearly destroyed by virtue; and this will come to pass in the age to come, until wickedness ceases; for what is defiled will be, instead of corrupted, destroyed; and impurity is destroyed either by practice or by severe chastisement. It is necessary to use this saying toward those who have been deemed worthy of divine things.

english: That they may not neglect the instruction, for many are being led away by wickedness into death; and those who are being killed in innocence unto death, you shall not spare to buy with your own blood; but if you give money or a beneficial word when asked, and if you say, 'I do not know this person,' you will be convicted of lying, and you will be guilty of two things—falsehood and murder; for the One who fashions breath also knows all things that He gives to each according to their nature: good to the good, and evil to the evil. For it is evident that reward is not according to quantity; for the sufferings of the present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to be revealed. But if anyone wishes to take hold according to quantity, let them suppose the recompense in proportion to each one's power, as also the gifts of the Spirit are given according to the proportion of faith. He who eats honey is the one who is benefited by the divine Scriptures; but the one who casts out the words from the things from which holy prophets and apostles have taken them, in doing and teaching, chews wax; and while eating honey is for the one who desires all things, eating wax is for the pure alone; or let honey be called the allegory, and wax, the literal exposition and investigation, in order to possess the hidden and deeper mind; for there is honey in the wax; and let the throat be the nourishing power of the soul, by which foods are conveyed into the belly; if therefore you accomplish these things—both those according to thought and those according to history—they will be to you a sensation of the wisdom itself, these wise doctrines; for if you find the spiritual mind of the Scripture, your end will be good, as it is said: 'Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of His saints'; do not abandon the hope for the future; do not prefer the devil to the righteousness of God, which the just possess; and do not let yourself be fed by deadly foolish reasonings, which is the belly; do not betray God for the sake of pleasure; for this one is the pasture of the righteous.

And he will not leave you. God indeed turns away his wrath from the one who has fallen, having shown mercy to him; but he is angry with the one who rejoices over the downfall of his enemy. For everyone who exults over a soul perishing is like the devil, who does not desire that all people be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. And indeed the Lord has commanded in the Gospels that we should pray for our enemies, that is, for all people. But the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, is not fleshly, that is, not perceptible to the senses. Now whoever is delivered to it while stumbling, their bones shall be broken by blows from above; and their bones shall be consumed by burning fire. Or whoever is delivered to it for repentance, shall be broken by the word of his wisdom like grain, so that he may become sweet bread. –The sword of God destroys those who are corrupted and worn away by the lusts of deceit, utterly consuming them. Or those who come from wickedness to the knowledge of God, it strips bare by the nerves from their evil deeds, so that, having put off the old man, they may clothe themselves with the new man created according to God, who is also impervious to demons, having been cleansed by the Lord, and abstaining from every wickedness. For he adds that they may become impervious like young eagles; or because those who have been burned and reduced to ashes ultimately become impervious to the eagles. For indeed, my words have been surrounded, and so on. –Who gathered the winds in his bosom? The swift mind of the wind has gathered faith from the east and west, north and sea, in the knowledge of God, and has given them spiritual contemplation to store up in the virtues. For the knowledge of God is the bosom of God, in which he embraces and prevails over all the godly, just as one might embrace gold in one’s bosom. –He who gathered from the east and west, north and sea, all the earthly nations, and condensed them by the virtues in the faith directed toward him, Christ God,

english: And one who stores away the heavenly water—the flowing water that comes from the fountain of life, that is to say, knowledge and wisdom, as Christ himself declares: “Whoever drinks of this water will never thirst again”—and also, “Whoever believes in me, from his innermost being will flow rivers of living water.” This one steals knowledge, not the one who receives what was beforehand prepared, but the one who takes away knowledge from false pretense. For indeed, all who have believed in Christ, receiving teachings from the holy prophets and apostles, are not called thieves of alien doctrines; for one steals another’s teachings in order to fill a hungry mind—but this was done before the appearance of the Savior. Now, however, Paul says: “Let the thief no longer steal, but rather let him work honestly, so that having acquired knowledge, he may share it with those in need.” For what is not ours and yet is ours, that we should steal it, we who have believed in Christ? For all things are ours, and we are Christ’s, through whom all things were made; and Christ is God’s. Therefore, banish the understanding of evil, do not again yield to wickedness; for everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin, and sin is now called the devil, the one who actively works iniquity. The offspring of evil, etc.—slander defiles the mind that utters it, and the mother of that, namely the soul, is not treated kindly. Vainglory makes the one who possesses it think himself just, without considering evil, though often he only does good things. Arrogance causes the one who possesses it to overlook poor friends.

Parents should, in like manner, dispense harsh foods to their children, so that the righteous and godly may be abhorred by them; they should be placed under restraint, and the parent himself should rise above such indulgence. For anger possesses entirely the one who harbors it, seeking nothing else but to compel evil-doing and punishment, to slander and insult, and never ceasing to act as a false accuser. Whoever conceives and carries out evil in action and thought, who corrupts his own mind or watches over another person with intent to harm, shall be accursed among the peoples of the angels and hateful among those of the nations who have been saved, when all shall become one flock and one shepherd. But those who reprove and correct through open confession of their own deeds, and who reflect upon the counsels of the better mind, shall be revealed as lofty before the Lord, proclaimed upon all things. Upon them shall come, in the present age, the good blessing of their works and the intellectual contemplation of wisdom; but in the age to come, the apportionment from the Lord. The one who walks behind the commands of God is built up in righteousness and holiness; for with wisdom a house is built, the soul and body prepared for the indwelling of God. Yet wisdom will not enter into a soul skilled in evil. For just as thorns destroy or livestock perish when there is no one to cleanse and guard, so too the foolish: wickedness is the goad that drives one toward those who beforehand prepare the way to the kingdom. A bulwark is an impassivity of the rational soul, composed of practical virtues; yet it is torn down and obliterated by the foolish person’s choice. Corruption loves these things: sordid gain, lust, and the harlot woman.

Indeed, these things have neither end nor satiety; there are three things that will be filled, and the fourth—she has not found it sufficient to say it is enough—namely, Sheol and the love of a woman, and the earth that is not satisfied with water; and fire, and water, they did not say, "It is enough." It continually receives the seeds, whatever you may cast down, and it longs for them. Thus, death and fire, upon the things they long for, they destroy. Such a thing is also poverty; these matters are consuming. Such a thing also is sloth and idleness. For perhaps someone wonders, why does Sheol not have satiety, even though it consumes humanity? For this reason, he says, these things also do not have satiety, nor do they stand still anywhere. But observe what has committed fornication with Sheol. These ravens—mystically they feed the righteous, but they punish the wicked, plucking out the eyes of injustice—because they laughed at the Father of all and God, and they dishonored the gracious knowledge that bore them. For the eye of the Father is the law given to us in righteousness by Him. And those who pluck out the eyes of the impious, He called ravens; but those who devour him entirely, He named eagles, because He trusts the former for partial purification, the latter for complete purification. For God wills even the impious to be saved. The rooster, the bird among us, is called "unwearied." And beside the females that associate with it, they are known as such; and the flocks of birds gather around it, perhaps because it circles around all.

english: He rejoices in pleasure; yet he is of good courage and turns himself wholly toward love in all things. Thus, the orders of the angels submit to the God of all, not only in fear but also in love, when He wills to perceive them as they obey His command and act upon it. Likewise, it is natural for the souls of the righteous to be so disposed: for all who place themselves under His command do not merely desire to know the mysteries and depths hidden in the Scriptures, which He approves of being known, but also whatever is destined to occur in human life—whether brought about by men or demons, whether through mental vision, by the grace of the divine Spirit granting foreknowledge, or through angelic instruction, or through the revelation of a vision. Here he calls the righteous "powers," those who possess strength against demons and passions, which he terms "spirit." Let them not drink from the cup that intoxicates the mind and clouds the senses with the harsh wine of heretics, which contains some knowledge contrary to the wisdom of God; lest, having drunk, they forget God’s wisdom and be unable to judge rightly or perceive the theory of knowledge, and thus fail to help themselves and the weaker in soul. To those who mourn in sin and ignorance, give them to drink from the Lord’s vineyard unto intoxication—that is, fasting, prayer, self-control, confession, and all things that bring joy to the soul; but to those in positions of authority, let them drink the pains of sin unto satisfaction, so that, having drunk, they may forget the demonic poverty. For the one who is intoxicated by the knowledge of the Lord forgets the practice of sorrows. He calls the poor the one deprived of knowledge.

Now then, concerning the corrupt and impure nature brought about by sin: the one who, through the spiritual word, puts to death the old man corrupted by deceitful desires, establishes his own mind in righteousness. This mind is said to be the throne of God, for wisdom and understanding have no other natural dwelling place but here; they do not sit elsewhere by nature. And righteousness, if not grounded in rational nature, cannot truly exist. All these things—the spiritual word, the renewed mind, righteousness, wisdom, understanding—are none other than Christ himself. You must be what you appear to be; do not pretend. Do not boast, but remain silent among the wise and listen attentively to the elders. Do not say, “I will set my throne above the stars, and I will be like the Most High.” Do not crave the chief seats, but fix your gaze on the lowest place. For it is better to be told, “Come up here,” than to be told, “Take the lowest place,” and be sent away in shame before the powerful. Do not pretend to be wise, nor deem yourself just. It is better that good things be spoken of you than that you speak them yourself. Therefore, God exalted him highly and bestowed on him the name above every name. He speaks of what has come before: our friend is God, who, because of his friendship toward us, became human. For he himself said to the disciples, “I no longer call you servants, but friends.” When a friend rebukes you, Christ says, because of this sin, avoid it; do not despise the rebuke, but withdraw and return to the original sound judgment—that is, to God’s loving kindness. He says, give thanks for God’s commandments; and friendship, he says, is the love toward God and neighbor. Let the one who loves God keep these commands within himself, so that he may not become twofold in distress before God.

When each receives what is due according to their worth, the Savior also says in the Gospels to the Jews who believed in him: If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples, and the truth has freed you from the curse of the law. Therefore, if friendship liberates, and the Savior liberates, and Christ is both truth and friendship, it follows that all who possess knowledge of Christ are friends to one another. Thus, concerning this friendship alone, those who are friends of the same person are friends, and others are also friends. The one who has been taught about the virtues and practices them guards his own possessions in a harmonious and mutually beneficial way. Place a precious sardius stone into a golden earlobe, and the wisdom of the Lord into an understanding that is impassive yet obedient to the Lord. Just as water flowing from snow in a dry place under heat brings benefit and refreshes the scorched, so God acts upon those who receive his knowledge, wisdom, and commandments. And just as snow melts under heat, so too does the counsel of the just dissolve the wickedness of the soul. As winds and clouds guide sailors upon the sea to prevent shipwreck, so the false knowledge of those in God’s wisdom prevents them from perishing along with those who boast in it. As bones give strength and security to the body, so the virtues have grown naturally within the soul. Yet these bones are shattered if not guarded against sins; some have called the spirited soul weak, for it breaks its own spiritual bones before God.

And it will perish on the day of judgment: a habit formed by the way, and an energy by the foot, will be perceived. Just as vinegar in a wound that has the beginning of corruption is incongruous, though it is food for sweetness, so the contemplation and conversation of a woman scatter the heart of the one who gives himself over to virtue and has a beginning. For what falls upon the heart is a passion, which is wickedness; and by its absence, some are called apathetic. –Grief is a corrupt privation of corrupt pleasure; but grief is also a praiseworthy privation of virtues and the knowledge of God. He says here that bread is the solid nourishment of the soul’s commandments; and drink, that it signifies divine knowledge; and coals of fire, that they are the gifts of the all-holy Spirit, which inflame and purify the wrinkles of men; for a coal of fire touched the lips of Isaiah’s seraphim at one time; and the one who has been cleansed, learns fieriness, and cries out to all: for by this kindness and beneficence, purifying oneself, the ruling part, you will make the fiery graces of the Holy Spirit compel him, not only to take hold, but also to make him your zealous worker in every good work, as if he had become your familiar friend before God in all things. He said the devil is a shameless person, stirring up the soul toward evil, and raising up, like northern clouds, evil thoughts against the soul; but everywhere Solomon says the tongue is the mind: therefore this person ought to be ashamed in judgment, which is not good.

Here then falls a righteous mind in the presence of Satan, accepting a corrupt line of reasoning, or a false doctrine. And one who turns away from the fountain of wisdom, rejecting its knowledge, and purifies the notions of the mind—these are called falls, and these are called risings, and these are called seats, and these are called standings, and these are called walks, and some of them are called stumbling blocks; and others are called hard and soft, and fragrant and foul, and sweet and bitter, and smooth and straight, and scholia. And again, some of its parts are called thorns and thistles, and others are called light and darkness, and life and death; and still others are called sickness and health, and again they are named falsehood and truth; and many other names does Scripture assign, both to the soul and to its notions. But a few things out of many are to be said: these are mind, soul, heart, man, male, female, slave, servant, father, son, spirit, eye, mouth, lips, tongue, larynx, belly, bosom, arm, finger, nostril, sheep, goat, shepherd, and many other names of the soul, which it is not now possible to set forth in detail. Counsel he spoke of here as the inclination of the heart toward the better: when someone does not call upon the divine help of God within himself, and forms a plan to do something good after reflection, but instead begins arrogantly and boastfully—it will not be completed, but rather what he undertakes will come to misfortune, because he has not surrounded himself with the divine aid of God for counsel.

Here he says the horse refers to the swift man who is receptive to learning, wisdom, and justice; but he is goaded by means of enigmas. The donkey, however, is pricked with a goad; the slow one among these hard sayings is pricked, instilling fear in them. But to the foolish nation, it is said they shall be struck with a rod, for he sets boundaries over the faithless servants or those under authority; the rod, after all, is a symbol of correction. From his own feet, etc. Here he says the feet are the servants; and shame comes upon the master from them, when he sends a message by a foolish messenger, or by counsel, or wisdom, or embassy, or alliance, or sympathetic words. For the foolish are defeated in all things; and indeed the Lord says in the Gospels: Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine. 17.240 Remove the foolish man’s evil way, and make his false knowledge long departed from him. Whoever gives knowledge to the foolish is like one who binds an honorless stone in a sling with gold; or like one who binds a precious stone in a sling and hurls it at stone-throwers. If the ecstasy of the foolish is shattered—by which they were estranged from God—then, having become clean again, they draw near to God; for all flesh shall see the salvation of God. But take heed here: that the souls purged of wickedness, he has called the flesh of the foolish; and so the Lord says: My spirit shall not remain in man forever, because they are flesh. english: He says, examining his own wickedness and turning back toward him, and then turning again toward him, he is like a dog eating its own vomit; just as was the wife of Lot, and she turned back toward what the unclean spirit had caused her to turn toward. This saying must be used against those who are reckoning some of the unworthy among the priesthood, or in the lot; for no one among us has established the justice and liberty of the Church; but it is either ours, or Christ’s, through which He judged Himself justified to be given over to slaughter, and His blood was poured out on her behalf; thus also every one who desires to undertake the oversight of the Church’s households must surrender himself, and seize the collar of the evil one, and liberate those under his wickedness, and bring them into the full knowledge of Christ. As fire in wood, so in evil thoughts the anger that is directed toward the passions of the mind blazes and burns; but where there is no double-mindedness, that is, no divided soul, but either to God or to mammon, stillness will come from it, the one over the other; either the commandment of God, having conquered, the evil one will be subdued, and he will make peace with wickedness; but if one chooses both, and falls out of life, and will be deprived of temporary things. The lips here he says are the thoughts; but the one who does not open the lips of the mind against the evil, confessing to God the evils which he has sown against God, but conceals them, covers his heart with grief, not thinking through folly that he has sin in these things; not knowing the God’s good compassion; for to those who thus endure and proclaim these things to Him, He awards crowns as if they were contending in each struggle through Him. He mocks, instead of rejoicing, he has taken; for a cheerful soul, delighting in the knowledge of the Scriptures, rejoices in being filled; but an impure soul, and the false knowledge, surely believes it to be true. Or the place of the heart, virtue and knowledge, from which a man, having been estranged, falls into wickedness and ignorance, and becomes a slave of sin, doing it; inasmuch as he is rational,

His place is virtue. An untroubled mind delights in varied pleasures—wisdom, knowledge, and hymnody; but a mind troubled by passion is shattered in ignorance and wickedness, and comes to a fall that is incurable and great. God is our friend and the friend of our forefathers, and of those who come after us; for he himself said, “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have hewn for themselves cisterns, broken cisterns.” Here Christ is our brother according to grace; but to enter your brother’s house without the commandments he has given us, in order to gain authority to enter his house—that is, to enter the kingdom of heaven—do not attempt it unhappily regarding these things; for such was the one who entered the wedding feast without a wedding garment; having been bound hand and foot, he was cast out of the wedding. Our brother here is the choir of angels; for according to the nature of the angels, before the transgression and fall, the devil was of the angels and of us; but God is our friend; and it is better to dwell with our true and genuine God, who is near and most closely present, than with one who has made himself far from himself a devil, as if submitting to a brother, in order to perish together with him. The one who joins with me through true knowledge is superior to the one who joins with me only through nature. english: Not only the angels, but also in the future time are under the Creator of the angels. For example, one does not drive away folly by dishonoring the fool, but by teaching him what disgrace folly brings upon itself; for indeed, confrontation directed at the person makes the sinner even more shameless. Of the words of God, some are written for the life of sons, others for the service of attendants. If one is courageous in impieties, then one is also courageous in virtues; and if the courageous person in impieties falsely accuses the poor, the courageous person in virtues encourages the poor. Therefore, everyone who comforts the poor in impieties, conspiring against them, slanders them before God—that is, opposes them with accusations—so that they may perish together with him. The lavish rain does not only destroy the fruits, but also lays waste the face of the earth, which bears the fruits; yet there is also a gentle rain, which makes the face of the earth healthy and nurtures and causes to grow the fruits within it. Thus, the lavish rain, by destroying the fruits, kills people, while the gentle rain, through the fruits, brings forth life. There is also a law that is lawless, and a law that is just. The lawless law destroys those who obey it; but the just law not only grants longevity of days, but also becomes a foretaste of the kingdom of heaven for those who submit to it, because it belongs to God. And everyone who loves God loves his law and keeps its precepts; and everyone who keeps the law attains divine possession and knowledge of God. But if those who love the law build walls for themselves, now the wall signifies insensibility and the knowledge of God.

These things alone by nature guard the rational nature. If wealth is the wickedness of the godless, and wise men shall destroy it, it is clear that the righteous and the wise destroy wickedness, through spiritual instruction leading the impure toward virtue. The law does not abhor anyone’s prayer, but the One who gave the law, God, regards the one who turns away his ear and causes the law not to hear as abhorrent. And Paul says: Foreseeing the future, Scripture instead says, “The One who gave Scripture foreknew the future.” The things sown in his heart by the evil one, if he does not declare them to the Lord God or to a God-loving person, will not prosper in the victory over the evil one; but the one who declares them shall be beloved by God and His angels. And James says: Confess your sins to one another, that you may be healed. And the Psalmist says: I will declare my iniquity before me to the Lord, and You forgave the wickedness of my heart. The revenues of the evil king are wickedness and false doctrines; for these things draw near to him those who are ruled by him. Moreover, those who obey the evil one falsely accuse God, because they are subject not to God but to His enemy, the devil. Since God hates the devil because of his evil works, He again, through His own works, exposes humanity to God. And the one who hates to wrong his own soul shall live the long time of the endless age. A man here, a murderer of the devil, he says:

He who becomes surety for injustice guarantees the presence of Satan. When one promises to Satan to deliver the fruits of iniquity—know that a lawless nation is the doctrine of demons, to which the educated son does not submit; by "son" he means the intellect. The one who suspends the mind from slipping into the wickedness of the evil nation, as if placing a savage collar upon it, prepares to receive an incorruptible world from the hand of the Lord as a private treasure for his soul. The one who cleanses himself from passions and labors to keep God’s commandments shall be filled with the bread of life—wisdom and divine knowledge. But the one who wastes leisure in neglecting God’s commandments shall be filled with poverty. Now the merciful, in the age to come, shall be shown mercy by God and become angels; they shall rule over the scoffers and the wealthy impious. Such a dignity the Lord also promised to give His disciples: to seat them on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. A throne is where the mind sits, full of spiritual knowledge, gathering those who have strayed from piety. To judge here means to teach. As also, "Open your mouth with God’s word, and judge all things soundly," means "teach." Moreover, know this: the merciful who overcomes the scoffer shall not himself become a scoffer, but will make the scoffer more merciful. If the impious cease to be impious, they shall become just; for the present destruction is the abolition of impiety.

english: This signifies that, just as the Lord called Matthew away from the tax office, He bestowed righteousness upon him; for the righteous increase whenever the wicked abandon their wickedness and become righteous along with those who are fervent in devotion. The righteous also groan and grieve, seeing the wicked standing in the place of wickedness, unrepentant. Indeed, a man who rebukes in the Lord’s discipline and instruction is better than one who urges in a hard heart, promising to share enjoyment with him in the burning; for when he is suddenly ignited in the desire of the passions, death that comes upon all arrives upon his fellow workers, and there is no healing for their souls. He did not say that healing would not exist after the fire is quenched, but that there is no healing while it burns, because it clearly has as fuel the substances of the passions—wood, grass, stubble—since, if it is true that health naturally grows after the burner for those who are being burned, then the same applies here. When the righteous are praised by the Lord on the day of judgment, the peoples of their share will rejoice; but those who are under the rulers and authorities, and the world-governors of this world, will then certainly groan. Here he speaks of the Father as God; but the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, seeing those who are called after Christ, following Him in deed and word and wisdom, and imitating Him, rejoices over them. And the good shepherd is a mind that possesses dispassionate thoughts; but if this is so, then a rash thought is a passionate thought, and a sheep is a dispassionate thought; therefore, the Lord sets those who are like goats on His left.

The sheep are on the right hand; he calls those who possess irrational souls goats, and in the same way he names those who have the tares among them tares, and those who possess the wheat, wheat, calling them by the name of their possession from the skilled and practiced habit of the hand; such also is what is said by Paul: Love does not boast, that is to say, the one who has love. Christ raises up the rational nature through his commandments, but the lawless Antichrist stirs up the human race toward destruction. In all things, judging is said to be teaching; for indeed, the one who judges between two or more concerning one thing teaches what is just and how to abstain from injustice; likewise, concerning virtues and every good thing, judging is said to teach; but a man here judging nations, he says, is Peter, who has taught the whole world the faith in Christ and godliness; and Paul, and the other teachers who came after; but a base man, those who follow Theodotus and Judas and the Samosatene and those of like mind with them; moreover, concerning the base man, David says: And they shall laugh at him, and they shall say: Behold the man who did not make God his helper. Men of blood are the demons, who have slain those living in Christ by shedding blood; but the upright will seek out his soul; these are those who wish to do and to understand what they themselves have practiced and conceived. Truly, the foolish man has an unrestrained temper; but this one is tempered in part, that is, becoming angry at things that are burning with passion. And toward the simpler ones, this must be said:

To those who are earnest, the one who through patience gradually consumes anger, bit by bit. To those who keep the law, the Lord will be an interpreter in the kingdom; but to those who break the law, there will not be an interpreter, but rather a punisher will be present. For no one is by nature hard-hearted; this is shown by the fact that, even if one understands, they do not obey. For the one who is by nature hard-hearted would never think anything correct at any time. I say this because of Pharaoh, who was hardened against Israel, and who was not instructed by words but by scourges. If indulgence leads to sin, and everyone who sins is a slave to sin, then everyone who indulges is a slave to sin. And on the last day, they will not grieve little over themselves. The Lord humbles the proud, but gives glory to the humble. —He says that pride is wickedness; and pride, along with the hunger it brings, causes destruction through wickedness to those who practice it, on the day of judgment. But to those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, the glory they gave God in hymns and by keeping His commandments will glory them. For glory is doing God’s commandments, as the Lord Himself says: “Those who glorify Me, I will glorify.” And wickedness begets pride in the rational soul. english: For just as the devil, having stolen the perfect man, offers him up in sacrifice, so too does the thief come only to steal, to sacrifice, and to destroy. For the thief says, "I do not come except to steal and to sacrifice and to destroy." — He spoke of the law as an oath: just as the oath places God in the soul, so the law brings God into the soul; and as perjury removes God from the soul, so lawlessness casts God out from it. Therefore, if, upon hearing the law established, we do not confess our sins before ourselves, being afraid and ashamed before men, we shall be brought to ruin. Thus David also says: "I said, I will confess my transgressions to the Lord concerning my iniquity, and You forgave the wickedness of my heart." And again: "Speak, you first, your sins, that you may be justified." And again Solomon says: "He who covers his wickedness shall not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes it shall find mercy." Those who fulfill the commandments minister to the angels, for they are our leaders, who received us from the beginning, when the Most High divided the nations and set the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God. And in ministering to our leaders, the angels, in the will of the Lord, in the judgment, there shall be right standing for us before the Lord on that day when He judges the inhabited earth in righteousness, if indeed the Father has given all judgment to the Son. Courage is the best habit of the rational soul, by which it has conquered and holds fast against its enemies. Having overcome the opposing power, we strip it, learning its words about it.

So that the evils associated with it may be made plain, those who are driven out by it— not only the simple-minded, but also those who have been made light-headed by indulgence— may easily flee from it. The soul trains itself upon wool and flax, exercising the discourses concerning both animate and inanimate things; or examining the discourses about practical and natural matters; or drawing the contemplation concerning bodies and incorporeal beings toward itself through practical habit. Or again, it finds the soul risen from night, watching, discovered by the Sun of righteousness, the Bridegroom; certainly, too, when it prays not to fall into temptation, saying, “I have kept watch and become like a solitary sparrow upon the housetop”; but food for the soul is the study of divine discourses, and its works are the virtues; its attendants are the senses. Thus, the soul more precious than costly stones provides these things to its bodily dwelling. It is said that the soul of the earnest one possesses the wood of knowledge and the wood of life of the Church— knowledge as law, life as word. For this soul is the one that came forth from Christ’s side, and having been found as His bride, she is the prudent and courageous woman who has kept this faith and again awaits this heavenly Bridegroom. A pure intellect is a noose, binding virtue to virtue and doctrine to doctrine; or it is a spoken word drawing spiritual contemplation from the intellect. Without such intellect, one cannot proceed nor come to be in contemplation of incorporeal things unless one has first set right what is within; for the disturbance of one’s own inner state tends to turn one back toward the things from which one came forth. But having acquired dispassion, one continues in contemplation through time,

And he will not worry about those in his house, for all who are with him are clothed: the one, anger, with gentleness and humility of mind; the other, desire, with self-control and continence. Hesitant grains—those things which make hesitation to obtain the kingdom—are eaten by the guileless and simple-minded soul that is well-knowing and God-loving; she does not eat them, nor does she even taste them, should she happen to desire them hastily; for she calls hesitant grains the evils. False pleasures and vain beauty: the most foolish soul not only conceives and imagines what is pleasing to itself, but also undertakes in action to fulfill the contemplation. But if the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, then the soul that happens to possess wisdom praises the fear of the Lord, which has become to her a foreigner in regard to such knowledge. For they know that she possesses the knowledge concerning practical matters—namely, the choice of virtue and the flight from vice—and that she has acquired as her possession those who are taught by her; therefore, they say, having taken hold of her, we handle these things thus. Otherwise, the possession of the righteous, wisdom and prudence, understanding and virtue—these possessions are seized by the impious, who persuade the righteous to do something of the things forbidden by God, so that the mind, blinded by sin, may fall away from these holy possessions. To the understanding righteous person, the burdensome things of affairs become easy; but to the one who is otherwise disposed, and who possesses ease and some manner of refreshment, the easy things become burdensome. For they possess a discourse that is knowledgeable in theorems, yet having nothing lofty.
